full_text:
Interviewer:	I’m trying to get a bit of background on why you’re doing engineering as well, so are you doing the mechanical?

Subject:	No, I’m doing manufacturing and design management.

Interviewer:	Right, OK, what A levels did you do?

Subject:	I did Maths, Physics, Biology and general studies ‘A’ level

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	School? Like a mixed comprehensive school.

Interviewer:	Normal.

Subject:	Yes, I suppose.

Interviewer:	You have got previous work experience haven’t you?

Subject:	Yes, yes I did my A levels and then I did a year in industry which was like a – do you know what that is? It’s like a nationwide scheme which focuses kind of – there’s about 6 different regions. There’s like northern region, midlands, southern and stuff and it’s – it kind of gets local companies to employ you for about a year and you have to do – it’s quite similar to this year on the course, ‘cos you have to do like an essay and you have to do lots of presentations and stuff and you get, just get the certificate. So I did that and then…

Interviewer:	How did you find out about that in the first place?

Subject:	Erm, I think it was posters in my A level college. I think there was posters. I think – it was like the end of my first year and I was sick of writing and I saw this poster saying oh try and get a job for you and I was like – I think I just went through there but it was quite a few years ago – I can’t remember – yeah, I think it was posters. And I just went like to the Open Day and then just. It was one of those things though you just kind of like – just end up kind of like having a go at it kind of thing.
Interviewer:	Who was the company that you went to work for?

Subject:	Erm, it was just this company called [name] Industries – it’s – I lived kind of in [town] and it was like on an industrial estate.

Interviewer:	Did you know, at that stage, that you wanted to do engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d applied to university to do engineering, so yeah – yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, What is it that made you want to do engineering, in the first place, then do you think?

Subject:	Erm, well it sounds stupid my dad’s an engineer at the moment. I think because I’ve got an interest in maths and physics and stuff and it just seemed the logical thing to go and do. Erm, I quite like knowing how things are made and how things work and things like that so - it’s quite a big area, it’s not just like being a teacher, it’s like vast and stuff.

Interviewer:	Yes. You said that your dad was an engineer, did he have much influence on your decision then?

Subject:	I think he influenced me in the way that he had a – he has a passion for engineering, so it kind of like encourages you to like think about engineering and kind of with dad, there’s a lot of stuff in the garage and he always let me go and play with it, but not in the sense that you’re going to do engineering at university – you know what I mean? He wasn’t like that.

Interviewer:	Did you have much careers advice or anything like that?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. I think at school we had the whole – you know those big forms where they tell you you’re gonna be like a gardener or something. They had those. Erm, I had quite a good careers advisor at my sixth form college – but that was more to do with like what I was gonna do at university and which universities to go to, rather than like what do you want to do with your life? Kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you would have gone into engineering if your dad wasn’t an engineer?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, yeah I would say so.

Interviewer:	I think you’ve been talking a bit about this already, but what is it that appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	Erm, the fact that when you go into work you could be doing like anything and it’s kind of like – it’s all about problem solving. So it’s (?) say, you never know what’s going to happen at work, during the day, and erm it’s quite hands on. You get to like look at stuff and you see where the problems are and you get to… I think – I don’t know, there’s just a lot of – there’s a lot of scope and it’s quite – it makes you think a lot and it stretches your brain.

Interviewer:	How did you decide to do the type of engineering that you are doing then?

Subject:	Erm, I actually started doing mechanical engineering and then I swapped so. I started doing mechanical engineering because it was just the maths and physics that I liked and that was the most obvious one to go into. Er, kind of like – I don’t know, got sick of doing maths and physics and realised that I actually wanted to do more like manufacturing (design?). Like I wanted to know how stuff was made more than the forces or anything like that.

Interviewer:	Did you do any of those sort of modules as part of your mechanical, that made you realise what it was like?

Subject:	Er, we did do a bit of manufacturing in the mechanical – it wasn’t really that much to be honest.

Interviewer:	Was it that aspect that got you interested in it then? That made you think…?

Subject:	Yeah, because like my gap year though was mainly like manufacturing. I mean the factories would – I wasn’t getting like a lot of high tech engineering calculations, it was more like looking at every day stuff, which is manufacturing and decided like oh well – a lot of the modules I was doing in my first year, in mechanical, it was like well, I haven’t used any of this in my gap year. Like I’m not learning about any processes or anything like that and I looked into manufacturing and decided that that was more the kind of field that I wanted to go into so thought it’d be more applicable.

Interviewer:	Ok, how did you decide to come to [this] University then?

Subject:	Erm, it was really (?) because I started doing my mechanical at [university] and it was like March sometime, I started looking at the courses and I think there was here and there was [university]. To some extent at [university] – they did manufacturing but that was quite close to where I was at home. I just came for an open day and I suppose – it was just really sunny and it was nice and I had a look around the department and everyone was really friendly and the course was like structured with what I wanted to do and I just thought it would be a good place to be.

Interviewer:	You think you should base your decision on how good the course is, but I went on the open days and I decided to go and look at [university], but the bit about the actual course is probably the worst one that they ever did but I liked the students union.

Subject:	Yeah, I know it’s just like little things like that make your mind up isn’t it?

Interviewer:	OK, did you realise that engineering was so male dominated?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did it bother you at all?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to take engineering?

Subject:	Yes, I think – I think it’s up to what you enjoy, and I don’t think they should like be put off to some extent. I’ve never had any – I don’t know, just.

Interviewer:	Do you think that maybe the reason why more women don’t do engineering is actually because they don’t know about engineering in the first place?

Subject:	Yes, certainly I’d say that it’s like that at school and we were quite lucky because we had erm – I did engineering at school, up in the 4th year, like product design at school do you know, in your like in art those kinds of things. So we were quite like open to it but I don’t – there’s a lot of girls kind of 14/15 year olds that probably don’t get exposed to it and then don’t get to think down that line of job to some extent.

Interviewer:	Do you think there should be more education in schools then?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely because I think that – it’s just getting more confidence in like at home and stuff as well, in doing stuff like jobs at home because I think they need to be encouraged and like loads of my female friends are like is this a screwdriver? They haven’t a clue what a screwdriver – it’s not really that hard but it’s just like general perspective. It’s like – if this makes sense – like media and general it’s like they’re thinking girls don’t know what to do and yeah, I think there should be a lot more.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Erm, being able to communicate; being able to oh you’ve made me think now (laughs). You need to be able to talk to people and not be scared of people and go and talk to managers and stuff. You need to be good at organising yourself because there’s a lot of different – you probably have a lot of different projects going at the same time. Erm, be able to think out of the box, to some extent and look at things from different perspectives. Erm, have good kind of like general physics knowledge and stuff like that. To know how the concepts of how things are going to perform. Erm…

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or more female?

Subject:	I think – I think they’re female from what like we’ve done on our course and our projects on the course, because females tend to be actually quite good at telling people what to do and organising people. And we always tend to like write up the reports because we get everything neat and tidy to some extent, whereas the guys are just like you know, whatever, we’ll chuck this in and stuff. Erm, I think to some extent the guys have a lot more – they have a lot more practical, like common sense to some extent, because I think, in general, they have had a better like when they were younger, kind of worked in the garage and stuff. They do seem to have a better general knowledge, to some extent, which helps them. Erm….

Interviewer:	Do you think that men make better engineers than women because of those skills, or is it important that women and men are both bringing those different aspects?

Subject:	Yeah, I think – it depends on the person because I know loads of guys that are crap engineers which – I mean because there’s a bigger proportion of men, you kind of get a better average whereas there’s only like 3 women and you can’t really – you can’t really compare like 3 girls on the course to – because it’s a smaller percentage. Erm, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	I think it’s easier to get things done in the workplace, being a female. I think – it’s like a session on the shop floor, it’s just like you want to go and get the job done, you can easily just go and they’ll go and do it and stuff. And I think you don’t really get told off as much as men do and I don’t think – because a lot of the men in engineering say oh like, you know you’re managers are going to be fifty or so, or sixty pushing it and they kind of of the age where you’ve got to be polite to them and stuff and I think I got away with quite a lot, to be honest (laughs). If I was a man I would have got like sacked for it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

Subject:	Yeah, I think some older men who’ve like been brought up in engineering, don’t like women engineers and they think that you don’t know anything, which is sometimes quite true. Er, I haven’t – to be honest, I’ve never really had any problems to some extent, you’ve just got to kind of go and show them that you can do something. It’s just that you’ve got to prove yourself to them, I think. I think that you’ve gotta like work harder and show that you actually do know something and you do use your initiative a bit more.

Interviewer:	OK. I’m going to ask you a bit about the course now – has the course been what you expected in terms of things like the skills you’ve been taught and the content of the course and gender proportions and anything like that?

Subject:	OK. Erm, yeah I think so. It’s a bit hard because we’ve learnt a lot about manufacturing and we do quite a lot of hours of that a week. We haven’t done as much kinds of proper hands on stuff, like being in a lab and using a lathe. We did that in our first year. We had like the labs and went generally in the workshops but – I had a fair amount of experience before, but like other people haven’t and for them to just use it for 2 hours wasn’t really developing their skills, it was just giving them an insight and stuff. So I was expecting it to be more, like actual make stuff, which we haven’t really done. Erm, comparing it to what I used to do in mech eng, the science has been a lot easier and it’s a lot more basic than what I was expecting. Erm, we’re not doing as much maths as what I thought we do because we only do maths in the first year. Erm, we’re doing like stats this year. I don’t know – I think it’s met my expectations, in what I’ve learnt, anyway.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Erm, the best thing has been the manufacturing lectures and there’s just – we’re just doing one on like prototyping which is really good and we got shown round the labs and shown how all the machines work – which is the best thing. Erm, the worst thing is going to 9 O’clock lectures. (Laughs) I don’t know – I don’t think we’ve had that many.

Interviewer:	That’s OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Yeah, we’ve got – the girl that we have – the woman that we have for stats and maths, last year, was female. Erm, …

Interviewer:	Have you noticed any differences in the types of subjects that they tend to teach or their styles of teaching at all? Do you think it’s…?

Subject:	Erm, the lady that teaches is – she talks a lot more to you, like more involvement and stuff and when she does maths. Yeah, there’s no like women in like heavy engineering stuff, really, I don’t think. No.

Interviewer:	Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, it wouldn’t do me any harm, would it?

Interviewer:	But do the lecturers treat you any differently?

Subject:	Hmm, I wouldn’t say so, no.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	He’s male.

Interviewer:	Would you prefer that they were female?

Subject:	Er, no, as long as they’re nice really and listen to you. I think that’s all you can ask for, probably.

Interviewer:	OK, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you, since you started the course?

Subject:	Oh I don’t know (laughs). I suppose – I’m not really sure – the guy who we’ve just had for philosophy I think. He was really good because she was like really enthusiastic and kind of like made you think about stuff, quite a lot. Yeah, I’ve not really had that many big influences.

Interviewer:	Have you had to do much group work at all?

Subject:	Yeah, there’s been quite a lot of group work.

Interviewer:	When you work in groups do you choose yourself who you want to work with or do you get put into groups?

Subject:	Erm, no, we don’t - we get put into groups by the lecturer.

Interviewer:	Does that bother you at all, would you rather choose who you work with?

Subject:	Yeah, I would rather choose who I work with, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. Would you rather work with women or men or aren’t you really bothered?

Subject:	I’d rather work with men.

Interviewer:	Why is that?

Subject:	Because the women on our course are all quite dictating. It’s like – it is quite – I do find it hard working with them because I think, in general, you tend to have similar qualities and it just gets quite difficult and it’s easy when it’s just one girl and a couple of men, in my sort of class, so…

Interviewer:	OK have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Erm, generally bad ones – because we normally do them like last minute and stuff and it’s always get quite stressful, right at the end. Erm, yeah, we just – we don’t always have good time management, so obviously it’s a bit stressful at the end of the project, really.

Interviewer:	OK, do the people you work with normally treat you the same as everyone else in the group?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Why did you decide not to go on the placement this time?

Subject:	Erm, because I’m too old. (laughs). Because I’m like 22 now, so it’s just gonna be a year out, I’d be like 24 by the time I graduated and I decided that I could just wait like another year and then probably get paid better than what I’d get paid next year. Yeah, I just wanted to graduate really.

Interviewer:	If you hadn’t already done a year out, might you have been more interested in it?

Subject:	Yes, definitely. I think it’s a really good thing to do and I think people should do it compulsorily – I think they should, before they have a proper job, have a …

Interviewer:	What type of work were you doing when you were on placement?

Subject:	Erm, well all the crap work, so – I used to erm, yes, cos on my gap year I did like 3 months on quality, 3 months in engineering and then I did about 6 months in purchasing. So in – in quality I had to like go down on the shop floor and – let me think – we had – yeah, we were doing like a reject analysis so we were trying to examine like whether, determine where the rejects were coming from so we could like lower those. So I had to like do loads of sheets and I was going get the sheets and then put all the information on the computers and stuff like that and pull up some graphs about what (lost words). In eng – in the engineering it - cos [name] industries is a – is a contractor, [company], contractor. They used to make – I’m not sure – like field hands – you know the big [diggers] and stuff (yeah) they used to make those. Erm, and [company] were wanting to go into like a different tyre. They wanted something cheaper and lighter, so I had to redesign the field tank and make some such, that was quite good – the prototype stuff. Erm general odds and sods jobs and stuff and erm the purchasing manager left – he got kind of sacked – and it was quite a small company, there’s only about 20 like engineers, like proper engineers there, so I got put in there to work with my other friend and we had to like manage that department for about 6 months. So that was pretty good.

Interviewer:	Were you given quite a lot of opportunities?

Subject:	Yeah, we were given quite a lot of responsibilities, quite early on and stuff which was good. Erm, yeah, that’s all I did there. And then I did a different place when I left Imperial, I worked in a plastics manufacturing company as a quality engineer, for about 4 months so I had my own kind of clients and I had some new projects coming into the factory, so I had to set up like and organise that the (tills?) were there and do this a bit like presentations and that kind of thing. And then dealing with all the quality issues that come in with that.

Interviewer:	Do you think at all that the past work you were given reflected the fact that you were a woman?

Subject:	Erm, no not really. I think – to some extent at [company] I had to like clean the pipes and do like – like checking the (davey?) amount and they used to get some lads to like lift the tanks and stuff like that. I was fairly – I was stronger than probably like most females and I think they kind of like didn’t give me very dirty jobs and stuff like that. ‘Cos I know the guy that used to work before me, at [company], he used to have to do a lot more manual work than me and stuff and if they were a bit down on the shop floor he used to have to like, go and use some of the presses and do some of the production – but I never used to do that.

Interviewer:	What do you think were the best and the worst things about the placement?

Subject:	Erm, 

Interviewer:	Or the experience generally?

Subject:	I think the best thing was just kind of like erm increasing my confidence – kind of like having a good understanding how everything works. ‘Cos I always used to think that like, any product that comes out of a factory is going to be spot on and there’ll be no problems with it and it really opened my eyes as to actually what goes on in a factory and stuff like that. Erm, the worst things – it was a really mundane job, and sometimes you’d just sit there all day and being like measurements and I used to hate doing that, because you keep the same thing (lost words).

Interviewer:	What types of skills do you think you’ve learnt from the experience?

Subject:	Er, I suppose like computer skills, using – I’ve learnt how to kind of use Excel, really, really well. Erm, I suppose time planning, although I’m still really crap. Erm, speaking – just like speaking to the clients and phoning up and knowing kind of what to say to them and stuff, I think. Erm, what else did I learn? General knowledge and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Would you say that you learnt more interpersonal skills than say the technical skills or was it … ?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely it wasn’t that technical.

Interviewer:	OK, have you used anything that you’ve learnt on your placement, back in the classroom environment?

Subject:	Erm, 

Interviewer:	Do you think that it’s helped you, coming to university, having had that experience?

Subject:	I think it’s given me good perceptives in like when we do stuff. It’s kind of like when you stand back and think, yeah but if you were doing this in industry it would be kind of different. (Yes) Kind of thing. Erm, it’s helped me in effect that when I worked for the plastic rolling company I got quite – I’ve learnt how the machines work quite a lot and stuff like that and had a good idea about plastics and pre project things like processing, and that helps me in like manufacturing modules and stuff. Erm. I don’t know. (laughs)

Interviewer:	Are you pleased that you did the placement before you started university?

Subject:	I think it helped me in the respect that I grew up quite a lot in that year, and I think if I’d gone to university straight after my A levels, I wouldn’t have got involved in as many things and stuff like that. I think I just grew up quite a lot. If I hadn’t – like probably if I hadn’t done like mech eng in the first year, I probably would have done one now because I’d just have that extra year, so – no, I’m glad I did it then.

Interviewer:	Do you think that, on the whole the educational experience, and the way that you’re taught reflects what it’s really like in the industry?

Subject:	OK erm, I don’t know. I suppose – I don’t know whether you know anyone – do you know anyone in engineering? In mech engineering?

Interviewer:	Not really, no.

Subject:	A few of like the lab technicians and the casting bloke have all had a lot of industry experience. So they kind of like – they teach from that perspective, which is good. Erm, a lot of the manufacturing lectures they have – they work in industry as well and they have to do projects in industry, so that – they kind of, in their lectures, reflect that as well then but…

Interviewer:	Do you think that helps people who haven’t had experience for when they do go into the work place?

Subject:	Erm, …

Interviewer:	Having that perspective?

Subject:	I don’t know. I think it helps them meet people that would be in industry – like they’re kind of similar to what you find in industry. I mean it helps them – it exposes them to other people, rather than lecturers, if you understand, but I’m not really sure. A lot of them don’t really have much clue about what you would do in industry to be honest.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it should be geared more towards getting a job at the end of it and the type of work that you will actually have?

Subject:	What, rather than doing stupid lectures?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Er, yeah, I suppose. I do think you have to do the science and you have to do other stuff to give you like the general knowledge, because people in the industry know about like fluids and if you had no idea about it – it’s likely to be like, what have you learnt kind of thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it would be better if there were more modules ‘hands on’?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely I think. Yes. 

Interviewer:	But that would still need to be a balance between…?

Subject:	Yeah, ‘cos you still need that kind of like – it’s different ways of making the same thing and doing like science and maths, you’re kind of taught a very different way. And doing other the stuff makes you think about different things – do you know what I mean?

Interviewer:	Do you know what type of company you’d like to work for when you’ve finished?

Subject:	No, I don’t know. I don’t want a job that relies on production and stuff. I don’t want people coming to me, like at 9 O’clock in the morning and saying right, you can get this stuff out the door by 2 O’clock. I don’t want anything like that. Erm, I’d just want something that kind of like stretches your brain and stuff and I’m quite interested in looking at and developing erm like manufacturing processes and finding better and more efficient and cheaper ways to do stuff. That kind of thing. I’m looking at kind of doing like more like research or R & D kind of stuff, rather than kind of working close to the shop floor.

Interviewer:	OK, what sort of things do you think will attract you to a company when you are looking for a job? Will it be pay or training opportunities?

Subject:	Yeah, things like training opportunities. Erm, yeah like what I’m gonna be able to do – like opportunities like within the companies whether I’m going to be able to travel with it and things like that.

Interviewer:	Would you like to travel?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d like to like be exposed to manufacturing in different companies, in different countries and see how it’s different and see if you can send that back to the UK or anything. Erm, location I suppose, money erm, and the general company ethos as well and what the kind of like the attitude of the company is as well, and like whether it’s kind of a bit backwards or a bit forwards and that kind of thing, I think.

Interviewer:	Do you think that type of attitude is to do with being a woman and how that affects how they are? It’s like females in a male world.

Subject:	I think to some extent, but just being treated as an equal but not because I’m a woman. I don’t know, like I don’t really get that sort of het up about being a woman engineer because I think, in general I haven’t really had any bad experiences and stuff and people do still accept you. It’s quite – no, there’s things like as long as they’re like encouraging and always trying to push you rather than – do you know what I mean? Just listening to you and like – I hate having managers that don’t listen to you and don’t really care about you – that kind of thing.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that work differs from university?

Subject:	Erm, it’s a lot harder. There’s a lot more time you spend at work. It’s like you only have like 18 hours a week, whereas at work you have like 35 or whatever. Erm….

Interviewer:	Do you think doing an engineering course – because it is quite structured, compared to other courses – I used to do about 6 hours a week – but do you think that’s a help when you go into the industry, that you have had more structured time than other students?

Subject:	Yeah, I think because we are generally in – although everybody’s getting to know us, we have got, you know, in most of the day. I think for some people, it probably is a shock to go into like 9 to 5 jobs from doing like 6 hours a week and stuff. Erm, so perhaps it’s easier to kind of get into it and stuff is a good thing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the way that you’re treated and what is expected of you differs at work?

Subject:	From?

Interviewer:	University.

Subject:	From university. Erm, yeah, I suppose so because here we’re kind of like left to our own devices for most of the time, unless your tutor’s on your back, whereas at work you’re gonna have people wanting your time, all the time really. You’re gonna have like – say you have you might have 3 different managers and stuff – they all want so many hours off you a week and it’s – I think it’s a lot more demanding being in a work environment, depending what you’re doing. I think you have shorter deadlines for stuff, like you also have like a week deadline or a day deadline or a few hour deadline whereas here we’ve got – we’ve kind of got, we know a month before whether we’ve got a course set deadline and stuff. So it’s not as time demanding. I think here we’ve got to like – you’ve got to use erm, you’ve got to be like a lot more self motivated because it’s long deadlines and you’ve got 12 weeks of lectures and if you don’t keep on top of your lectures, then by the time you get to exams you can have like piles of work to do. Erm, whereas I think in work, while you have to be self-motivated you don’t have to be as self-motivated.

Interviewer:	Yes, I know what you mean. At university it would be easy to leave things for a long period of time, in work there’s shorter deadlines.

Subject:	Yeah, you’ve got to kind of – it’s like obviously you get sacked into your work, whereas here you just kind of scrape through exams and get like a third don’t you?

Interviewer:	What skills do you think you’ll take from being at university to – or from what you’ve learnt at university, to industry?

Subject:	OK, I think like self-motivation is a big thing. I think being able to like – someone give you a project and get on with it and stuff like that. Erm, I don’t know. I think …

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s more about the interpersonal skills or using the technical skills or they’re both important?

Subject:	What at university or…?

Interviewer:	Yeah, take what you’ve learnt at university to take into industry?

Subject:	Oh OK. Yeah, it is ‘cos I was kind of like on a few committees and stuff like that, and I suppose that’s going to help like being in meetings with people but that’s kind of not really my course stuff but in general university those kind of skills, yes, I’d say that I’ve learnt quite a lot in stuff like organising and planning stuff.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university experience, in general, does prepare you for the workplace?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. I think people that do ‘A’ levels or whatever and then just kind of stay at home and then eventually move out, kind of take a long time to develop, whereas at university you’re just going to get thrown into it and you have to like stand on your own 2 feet, quite early on to some extent.

Interviewer:	OK In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 2 years time?

Subject:	Erm, I think that I’ll be like my first job after graduation, so I don’t know it’s – hopefully with a decent job, hopefully with a job that I enjoy. Erm, 

Interviewer:	Is that in engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d say I’d have a job in engineering, yeah.

Interviewer:	What about more long term, say in 5 or10 years time?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know really. Ooh, I don’t know because it all depends on whether – because I think women have the whole like husband and children stuff and that sort of breaks your career up as well, so – I don’t know ‘cos – I don’t really – I really don’t know.

Interviewer:	Do you think that, when it comes to like having a family and things like that, do you think there’s actually more conflict between family and career because of the type of industry that you’ve chosen?

Subject:	Erm, it’s erm – I can’t see myself – I do think that erm you probably don’t have the kind of work but I don’t really like to put children into bases. I do think the first 5 years you need to kind of like be with children and stuff. But I would like to go back and I don’t – I know that I couldn’t stand being at home all day, every day. And perhaps even like – if I had children – I’d probably have some kind of project at home, and perhaps like work from home to some extent which is – although you can’t do that all day. I wouldn’t be surprised if I was still in engineering in 10 years time. I wouldn’t be surprised if I did something else though. It depends though, what opportunities you get, I think.

Interviewer:	Yeah, do you think that the career prospects are good in that field of engineering?

Subject:	Yes, I would think so. I think if you – like in the next 5 or 8 years or so, kind of like followed a good career path and kind of developed your knowledge and skills and stuff, I think in the future you could go quite far.

Interviewer:	Are you interested in managerial type side of things?

Subject:	Er, to some extent yeah, I quite enjoy project management. I do enjoy like when we have like projects on the course, kind of like telling the boys what to do. (laughter) So I would like to do like manager – I wouldn’t have any problems with managing like a team of colleagues or anything like that so…

Interviewer:	Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Is there anything that you would you do differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	Erm, no I think I am happy with how I’ve ended up. I think the only thing I would have liked to have done, is perhaps, in my gap year got sponsored and that would’ve like taken the stress off money and stuff but I think – no, I can’t imagine not doing what I’ve done – so.

Interviewer:	Would you rather have maybe come straight to [this university] or do you think that it’s…?

Subject:	No, I think going to [university] was quite a good thing for me. I mean I really enjoyed it. I’ve really enjoyed my time there and I made some like friends which I can’t imagine not having and stuff and erm I did learn a few things while I was there (laughter) that kind of thing. Erm, no, I wouldn’t really change it really.

Interviewer:	You mentioned about the salary, being sponsored, and that you’d have liked to have been sponsored (yeah). What do you think are the main advantages of being sponsored?

Subject:	Not having the stress of finding jobs in the summer. Erm, like you know that at the end of year you’re gonna have like a job where you’re gonna get like a few grand in the summer. I suppose, to some extent, you know, it opens up the opportunities like when you graduate and stuff and I’ve seen all my friends, in the year above me, applying for jobs this year and it’s taken them so long and it would’ve have been nice to have that pressure not on me, for next year, but I think.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

Subject:	Yeah, you’re kind of constrained. You can’t like have summer off if you want to go and do something else – you can’t have that. And then you might – I mean, with sponsorship you can get into the aspect of having to sign your life away for a few years and stuff, which, I don’t think’s a good idea when you’ve kind of got another 3 years of education and you’re kind of like – you could be anywhere by the end of that. It’s a bit constraining.

Interviewer:	So how come you didn’t do get sponsorship? Were you given the opportunity on your course?

Subject:	Erm, the students like the company that I went with, in my gap year, didn’t sponsor – so not a lot of them sponsored anyway. It’s just (a few?) that’s involved.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics and culture of the engineering industry?

Subject:	OK, erm, (pause) I don’t know really – like describe the culture and…?

Interviewer:	The characteristics.

Subject:	OK. Well, it can be fast moving, I suppose (yes). I suppose it’s busy that it’s fast moving – kind of like busy. Kind of like fast developing – there’s always like new things being made and that kind of thing. Erm, it’s a bit loud and noisy and oily and messy. Erm, I suppose male dominated – it is male dominated and erm perhaps undervalued by general society. If you say you’re engineer, they don’t really understand what you actually do kind of thing.

Interviewer:	OK, why do you think it is so male dominated?

Subject:	Sorry?

Interviewer:	Why do you think that it is so male dominated?

Subject:	It’s just a man’s job. It’s not a man’s job but it’s been – it’s more manual as in you have to like – well, it’s just sort of like from years and years ago,, isn’t it? That’s what the men did and that’s what the women did and it’s just kind of going along that path really and slowly starting to merge with women, I think.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the perception of the industry is why there aren’t more women in the industry?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so. Erm, but then, like loads of my female friends wouldn’t even – I don’t think they would really be interested in being engineers and stuff and to some extent. Without sounding sexist and women are like that, and men are like that, to some extent, and then you have like the grey area, if that makes sense. I think a lot of my female friends wouldn’t even – they wouldn’t enjoy it I don’t think. I don’t think – I don’t know – they’re not interested enough, I think.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that any aspects of the engineering culture might be problematic for you?

Subject:	Erm, like what?

Interviewer:	Like the fact that it is so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, no, not really.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s it then, thank you very much.

turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: School? Like a mixed comprehensive school.

turns.text: Yes. You said that your dad was an engineer, did he have much influence on your decision then?

turns.speaker: Interviewer

turns.speaker: Interviewer

Like I wanted to know how stuff was made more than the forces or anything like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do any of those sort of modules as part of your mechanical, that made you realise what it was like?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, we did do a bit of manufacturing in the mechanical – it wasn’t really that much to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it that aspect that got you interested in it then? That made you think…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because like my gap year though was mainly like manufacturing. Like I’m not learning about any processes or anything like that and I looked into manufacturing and decided that that was more the kind of field that I wanted to go into so thought it’d be more applicable.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, how did you decide to come to [this] University then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it was really (?) because I started doing my mechanical at [university] and it was like March sometime, I started looking at the courses and I think there was here and there was [university]. To some extent at [university] – they did manufacturing but that was quite close to where I was at home. I just came for an open day and I suppose – it was just really sunny and it was nice and I had a look around the department and everyone was really friendly and the course was like structured with what I wanted to do and I just thought it would be a good place to be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You think you should base your decision on how good the course is, but I went on the open days and I decided to go and look at [university], but the bit about the actual course is probably the worst one that they ever did but I liked the students union.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I know it’s just like little things like that make your mind up isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you realise that engineering was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to take engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think – I think it’s up to what you enjoy, and I don’t think they should like be put off to some extent. I’ve never had any – I don’t know, just.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that maybe the reason why more women don’t do engineering is actually because they don’t know about engineering in the first place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, certainly I’d say that it’s like that at school and we were quite lucky because we had erm – I did engineering at school, up in the 4th year, like product design at school do you know, in your like in art those kinds of things. So we were quite like open to it but I don’t – there’s a lot of girls kind of 14/15 year olds that probably don’t get exposed to it and then don’t get to think down that line of job to some extent.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there should be more education in schools then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely because I think that – it’s just getting more confidence in like at home and stuff as well, in doing stuff like jobs at home because I think they need to be encouraged and like loads of my female friends are like is this a screwdriver? They haven’t a clue what a screwdriver – it’s not really that hard but it’s just like general perspective. It’s like – if this makes sense – like media and general it’s like they’re thinking girls don’t know what to do and yeah, I think there should be a lot more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, being able to communicate; being able to oh you’ve made me think now (laughs). You need to be able to talk to people and not be scared of people and go and talk to managers and stuff. You need to be good at organising yourself because there’s a lot of different – you probably have a lot of different projects going at the same time. Erm, be able to think out of the box, to some extent and look at things from different perspectives. Erm, have good kind of like general physics knowledge and stuff like that. To know how the concepts of how things are going to perform. Erm…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or more female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think – I think they’re female from what like we’ve done on our course and our projects on the course, because females tend to be actually quite good at telling people what to do and organising people. And we always tend to like write up the reports because we get everything neat and tidy to some extent, whereas the guys are just like you know, whatever, we’ll chuck this in and stuff. Erm, I think to some extent the guys have a lot more – they have a lot more practical, like common sense to some extent, because I think, in general, they have had a better like when they were younger, kind of worked in the garage and stuff. They do seem to have a better general knowledge, to some extent, which helps them. Erm….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that men make better engineers than women because of those skills, or is it important that women and men are both bringing those different aspects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think – it depends on the person because I know loads of guys that are crap engineers which – I mean because there’s a bigger proportion of men, you kind of get a better average whereas there’s only like 3 women and you can’t really – you can’t really compare like 3 girls on the course to – because it’s a smaller percentage. Erm, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any advantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s easier to get things done in the workplace, being a female. I think – it’s like a session on the shop floor, it’s just like you want to go and get the job done, you can easily just go and they’ll go and do it and stuff. And I think you don’t really get told off as much as men do and I don’t think – because a lot of the men in engineering say oh like, you know you’re managers are going to be fifty or so, or sixty pushing it and they kind of of the age where you’ve got to be polite to them and stuff and I think I got away with quite a lot, to be honest (laughs). If I was a man I would have got like sacked for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think some older men who’ve like been brought up in engineering, don’t like women engineers and they think that you don’t know anything, which is sometimes quite true. Er, I haven’t – to be honest, I’ve never really had any problems to some extent, you’ve just got to kind of go and show them that you can do something. It’s just that you’ve got to prove yourself to them, I think. I think that you’ve gotta like work harder and show that you actually do know something and you do use your initiative a bit more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. I’m going to ask you a bit about the course now – has the course been what you expected in terms of things like the skills you’ve been taught and the content of the course and gender proportions and anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK. Erm, yeah I think so. It’s a bit hard because we’ve learnt a lot about manufacturing and we do quite a lot of hours of that a week. We haven’t done as much kinds of proper hands on stuff, like being in a lab and using a lathe. We did that in our first year. We had like the labs and went generally in the workshops but – I had a fair amount of experience before, but like other people haven’t and for them to just use it for 2 hours wasn’t really developing their skills, it was just giving them an insight and stuff. So I was expecting it to be more, like actual make stuff, which we haven’t really done. Erm, comparing it to what I used to do in mech eng, the science has been a lot easier and it’s a lot more basic than what I was expecting. Erm, we’re not doing as much maths as what I thought we do because we only do maths in the first year. Erm, we’re doing like stats this year. I don’t know – I think it’s met my expectations, in what I’ve learnt, anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the best thing has been the manufacturing lectures and there’s just – we’re just doing one on like prototyping which is really good and we got shown round the labs and shown how all the machines work – which is the best thing. Erm, the worst thing is going to 9 O’clock lectures. (Laughs) I don’t know – I don’t think we’ve had that many.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, we’ve got – the girl that we have – the woman that we have for stats and maths, last year, was female. Erm, …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you noticed any differences in the types of subjects that they tend to teach or their styles of teaching at all? Do you think it’s…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the lady that teaches is – she talks a lot more to you, like more involvement and stuff and when she does maths. Yeah, there’s no like women in like heavy engineering stuff, really, I don’t think. No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, it wouldn’t do me any harm, would it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But do the lecturers treat you any differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I wouldn’t say so, no.

turns.text: OK, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.text: Would you prefer that they were female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, no, as long as they’re nice really and listen to you. I think that’s all you can ask for, probably.

turns.text: OK, who or what do you think has been the biggest influence on you, since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I don’t know (laughs). I suppose – I’m not really sure – the guy who we’ve just had for philosophy I think. He was really good because she was like really enthusiastic and kind of like made you think about stuff, quite a lot. Yeah, I’ve not really had that many big influences.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that bother you at all, would you rather choose who you work with?

turns.text: Yeah, I would rather choose who I work with, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Would you rather work with women or men or aren’t you really bothered?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.text: Why is that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because the women on our course are all quite dictating. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, generally bad ones – because we normally do them like last minute and stuff and it’s always get quite stressful, right at the end. Erm, yeah, we just – we don’t always have good time management, so obviously it’s a bit stressful at the end of the project, really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do the people you work with normally treat you the same as everyone else in the group?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why did you decide not to go on the placement this time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, because I’m too old. (laughs). Because I’m like 22 now, so it’s just gonna be a year out, I’d be like 24 by the time I graduated and I decided that I could just wait like another year and then probably get paid better than what I’d get paid next year. Yeah, I just wanted to graduate really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you hadn’t already done a year out, might you have been more interested in it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely. I think it’s a really good thing to do and I think people should do it compulsorily – I think they should, before they have a proper job, have a …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What type of work were you doing when you were on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well all the crap work, so – I used to erm, yes, cos on my gap year I did like 3 months on quality, 3 months in engineering and then I did about 6 months in purchasing. So in – in quality I had to like go down on the shop floor and – let me think – we had – yeah, we were doing like a reject analysis so we were trying to examine like whether, determine where the rejects were coming from so we could like lower those. So I had to like do loads of sheets and I was going get the sheets and then put all the information on the computers and stuff like that and pull up some graphs about what (lost words). In eng – in the engineering it - cos [name] industries is a – is a contractor, [company], contractor. They used to make – I’m not sure – like field hands – you know the big [diggers] and stuff (yeah) they used to make those. Erm, and [company] were wanting to go into like a different tyre. They wanted something cheaper and lighter, so I had to redesign the field tank and make some such, that was quite good – the prototype stuff. Erm general odds and sods jobs and stuff and erm the purchasing manager left – he got kind of sacked – and it was quite a small company, there’s only about 20 like engineers, like proper engineers there, so I got put in there to work with my other friend and we had to like manage that department for about 6 months. So that was pretty good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you given quite a lot of opportunities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, we were given quite a lot of responsibilities, quite early on and stuff which was good. Erm, yeah, that’s all I did there. And then I did a different place when I left Imperial, I worked in a plastics manufacturing company as a quality engineer, for about 4 months so I had my own kind of clients and I had some new projects coming into the factory, so I had to set up like and organise that the (tills?) were there and do this a bit like presentations and that kind of thing. And then dealing with all the quality issues that come in with that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think at all that the past work you were given reflected the fact that you were a woman?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no not really. I think – to some extent at [company] I had to like clean the pipes and do like – like checking the (davey?) amount and they used to get some lads to like lift the tanks and stuff like that. I was fairly – I was stronger than probably like most females and I think they kind of like didn’t give me very dirty jobs and stuff like that. ‘Cos I know the guy that used to work before me, at [company], he used to have to do a lot more manual work than me and stuff and if they were a bit down on the shop floor he used to have to like, go and use some of the presses and do some of the production – but I never used to do that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think were the best and the worst things about the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or the experience generally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the best thing was just kind of like erm increasing my confidence – kind of like having a good understanding how everything works. ‘Cos I always used to think that like, any product that comes out of a factory is going to be spot on and there’ll be no problems with it and it really opened my eyes as to actually what goes on in a factory and stuff like that. Erm, the worst things – it was a really mundane job, and sometimes you’d just sit there all day and being like measurements and I used to hate doing that, because you keep the same thing (lost words).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What types of skills do you think you’ve learnt from the experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I suppose like computer skills, using – I’ve learnt how to kind of use Excel, really, really well. Erm, I suppose time planning, although I’m still really crap. Erm, speaking – just like speaking to the clients and phoning up and knowing kind of what to say to them and stuff, I think. Erm, what else did I learn? General knowledge and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you say that you learnt more interpersonal skills than say the technical skills or was it … ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely it wasn’t that technical.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you used anything that you’ve learnt on your placement, back in the classroom environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it’s helped you, coming to university, having had that experience?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s given me good perceptives in like when we do stuff. It’s kind of like when you stand back and think, yeah but if you were doing this in industry it would be kind of different. (Yes) Kind of thing. Erm, it’s helped me in effect that when I worked for the plastic rolling company I got quite – I’ve learnt how the machines work quite a lot and stuff like that and had a good idea about plastics and pre project things like processing, and that helps me in like manufacturing modules and stuff. Erm. I don’t know. (laughs)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you pleased that you did the placement before you started university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it helped me in the respect that I grew up quite a lot in that year, and I think if I’d gone to university straight after my A levels, I wouldn’t have got involved in as many things and stuff like that. I think I just grew up quite a lot. If I hadn’t – like probably if I hadn’t done like mech eng in the first year, I probably would have done one now because I’d just have that extra year, so – no, I’m glad I did it then.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that, on the whole the educational experience, and the way that you’re taught reflects what it’s really like in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK erm, I don’t know. I suppose – I don’t know whether you know anyone – do you know anyone in engineering? In mech engineering?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not really, no.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A few of like the lab technicians and the casting bloke have all had a lot of industry experience. So they kind of like – they teach from that perspective, which is good. Erm, a lot of the manufacturing lectures they have – they work in industry as well and they have to do projects in industry, so that – they kind of, in their lectures, reflect that as well then but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that helps people who haven’t had experience for when they do go into the work place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Having that perspective?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. I think it helps them meet people that would be in industry – like they’re kind of similar to what you find in industry. I mean it helps them – it exposes them to other people, rather than lecturers, if you understand, but I’m not really sure. A lot of them don’t really have much clue about what you would do in industry to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it should be geared more towards getting a job at the end of it and the type of work that you will actually have?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What, rather than doing stupid lectures?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah, I suppose. I do think you have to do the science and you have to do other stuff to give you like the general knowledge, because people in the industry know about like fluids and if you had no idea about it – it’s likely to be like, what have you learnt kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it would be better if there were more modules ‘hands on’?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely I think. Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But that would still need to be a balance between…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, ‘cos you still need that kind of like – it’s different ways of making the same thing and doing like science and maths, you’re kind of taught a very different way. And doing other the stuff makes you think about different things – do you know what I mean?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know what type of company you’d like to work for when you’ve finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t know. I don’t want a job that relies on production and stuff. I don’t want people coming to me, like at 9 O’clock in the morning and saying right, you can get this stuff out the door by 2 O’clock. I don’t want anything like that. Erm, I’d just want something that kind of like stretches your brain and stuff and I’m quite interested in looking at and developing erm like manufacturing processes and finding better and more efficient and cheaper ways to do stuff. That kind of thing. I’m looking at kind of doing like more like research or R & D kind of stuff, rather than kind of working close to the shop floor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what sort of things do you think will attract you to a company when you are looking for a job? Will it be pay or training opportunities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, things like training opportunities. Erm, yeah like what I’m gonna be able to do – like opportunities like within the companies whether I’m going to be able to travel with it and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to travel?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’d like to like be exposed to manufacturing in different companies, in different countries and see how it’s different and see if you can send that back to the UK or anything. Erm, location I suppose, money erm, and the general company ethos as well and what the kind of like the attitude of the company is as well, and like whether it’s kind of a bit backwards or a bit forwards and that kind of thing, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that type of attitude is to do with being a woman and how that affects how they are? It’s like females in a male world.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think to some extent, but just being treated as an equal but not because I’m a woman. I don’t know, like I don’t really get that sort of het up about being a woman engineer because I think, in general I haven’t really had any bad experiences and stuff and people do still accept you. It’s quite – no, there’s things like as long as they’re like encouraging and always trying to push you rather than – do you know what I mean? Just listening to you and like – I hate having managers that don’t listen to you and don’t really care about you – that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that work differs from university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it’s a lot harder. There’s a lot more time you spend at work. It’s like you only have like 18 hours a week, whereas at work you have like 35 or whatever. Erm….

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think doing an engineering course – because it is quite structured, compared to other courses – I used to do about 6 hours a week – but do you think that’s a help when you go into the industry, that you have had more structured time than other students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think because we are generally in – although everybody’s getting to know us, we have got, you know, in most of the day. I think for some people, it probably is a shock to go into like 9 to 5 jobs from doing like 6 hours a week and stuff. Erm, so perhaps it’s easier to kind of get into it and stuff is a good thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the way that you’re treated and what is expected of you differs at work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: From?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: University.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: From university. Erm, yeah, I suppose so because here we’re kind of like left to our own devices for most of the time, unless your tutor’s on your back, whereas at work you’re gonna have people wanting your time, all the time really. You’re gonna have like – say you have you might have 3 different managers and stuff – they all want so many hours off you a week and it’s – I think it’s a lot more demanding being in a work environment, depending what you’re doing. I think you have shorter deadlines for stuff, like you also have like a week deadline or a day deadline or a few hour deadline whereas here we’ve got – we’ve kind of got, we know a month before whether we’ve got a course set deadline and stuff. So it’s not as time demanding. I think here we’ve got to like – you’ve got to use erm, you’ve got to be like a lot more self motivated because it’s long deadlines and you’ve got 12 weeks of lectures and if you don’t keep on top of your lectures, then by the time you get to exams you can have like piles of work to do. Erm, whereas I think in work, while you have to be self-motivated you don’t have to be as self-motivated.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, I know what you mean. At university it would be easy to leave things for a long period of time, in work there’s shorter deadlines.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, you’ve got to kind of – it’s like obviously you get sacked into your work, whereas here you just kind of scrape through exams and get like a third don’t you?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What skills do you think you’ll take from being at university to – or from what you’ve learnt at university, to industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK, I think like self-motivation is a big thing. I think being able to like – someone give you a project and get on with it and stuff like that. Erm, I don’t know. I think …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s more about the interpersonal skills or using the technical skills or they’re both important?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What at university or…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, take what you’ve learnt at university to take into industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh OK. Yeah, it is ‘cos I was kind of like on a few committees and stuff like that, and I suppose that’s going to help like being in meetings with people but that’s kind of not really my course stuff but in general university those kind of skills, yes, I’d say that I’ve learnt quite a lot in stuff like organising and planning stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university experience, in general, does prepare you for the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. I think people that do ‘A’ levels or whatever and then just kind of stay at home and then eventually move out, kind of take a long time to develop, whereas at university you’re just going to get thrown into it and you have to like stand on your own 2 feet, quite early on to some extent.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 2 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think that I’ll be like my first job after graduation, so I don’t know it’s – hopefully with a decent job, hopefully with a job that I enjoy. Erm,

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’d say I’d have a job in engineering, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about more long term, say in 5 or10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know really. Ooh, I don’t know because it all depends on whether – because I think women have the whole like husband and children stuff and that sort of breaks your career up as well, so – I don’t know ‘cos – I don’t really – I really don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that, when it comes to like having a family and things like that, do you think there’s actually more conflict between family and career because of the type of industry that you’ve chosen?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it’s erm – I can’t see myself – I do think that erm you probably don’t have the kind of work but I don’t really like to put children into bases. I do think the first 5 years you need to kind of like be with children and stuff. But I would like to go back and I don’t – I know that I couldn’t stand being at home all day, every day. And perhaps even like – if I had children – I’d probably have some kind of project at home, and perhaps like work from home to some extent which is – although you can’t do that all day. I wouldn’t be surprised if I was still in engineering in 10 years time. I wouldn’t be surprised if I did something else though. It depends though, what opportunities you get, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think that the career prospects are good in that field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I would think so. I think if you – like in the next 5 or 8 years or so, kind of like followed a good career path and kind of developed your knowledge and skills and stuff, I think in the future you could go quite far.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you interested in managerial type side of things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, to some extent yeah, I quite enjoy project management. I do enjoy like when we have like projects on the course, kind of like telling the boys what to do. (laughter) So I would like to do like manager – I wouldn’t have any problems with managing like a team of colleagues or anything like that so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Is there anything that you would you do differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no I think I am happy with how I’ve ended up. I think the only thing I would have liked to have done, is perhaps, in my gap year got sponsored and that would’ve like taken the stress off money and stuff but I think – no, I can’t imagine not doing what I’ve done – so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have maybe come straight to [this university] or do you think that it’s…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think going to [university] was quite a good thing for me. I mean I really enjoyed it. I’ve really enjoyed my time there and I made some like friends which I can’t imagine not having and stuff and erm I did learn a few things while I was there (laughter) that kind of thing. Erm, no, I wouldn’t really change it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You mentioned about the salary, being sponsored, and that you’d have liked to have been sponsored (yeah). What do you think are the main advantages of being sponsored?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not having the stress of finding jobs in the summer. Erm, like you know that at the end of year you’re gonna have like a job where you’re gonna get like a few grand in the summer. I suppose, to some extent, you know, it opens up the opportunities like when you graduate and stuff and I’ve seen all my friends, in the year above me, applying for jobs this year and it’s taken them so long and it would’ve have been nice to have that pressure not on me, for next year, but I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any disadvantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, you’re kind of constrained. You can’t like have summer off if you want to go and do something else – you can’t have that. And then you might – I mean, with sponsorship you can get into the aspect of having to sign your life away for a few years and stuff, which, I don’t think’s a good idea when you’ve kind of got another 3 years of education and you’re kind of like – you could be anywhere by the end of that. It’s a bit constraining.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So how come you didn’t do get sponsorship? Were you given the opportunity on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, the students like the company that I went with, in my gap year, didn’t sponsor – so not a lot of them sponsored anyway. It’s just (a few?) that’s involved.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics and culture of the engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK, erm, (pause) I don’t know really – like describe the culture and…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The characteristics.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK. Well, it can be fast moving, I suppose (yes). I suppose it’s busy that it’s fast moving – kind of like busy. Kind of like fast developing – there’s always like new things being made and that kind of thing. Erm, it’s a bit loud and noisy and oily and messy. Erm, I suppose male dominated – it is male dominated and erm perhaps undervalued by general society. If you say you’re engineer, they don’t really understand what you actually do kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why do you think it is so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sorry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that it is so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s just a man’s job. It’s not a man’s job but it’s been – it’s more manual as in you have to like – well, it’s just sort of like from years and years ago,, isn’t it? That’s what the men did and that’s what the women did and it’s just kind of going along that path really and slowly starting to merge with women, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the perception of the industry is why there aren’t more women in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so. Erm, but then, like loads of my female friends wouldn’t even – I don’t think they would really be interested in being engineers and stuff and to some extent. Without sounding sexist and women are like that, and men are like that, to some extent, and then you have like the grey area, if that makes sense. I think a lot of my female friends wouldn’t even – they wouldn’t enjoy it I don’t think. I don’t think – I don’t know – they’re not interested enough, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that any aspects of the engineering culture might be problematic for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, like what?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like the fact that it is so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no, not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s it then, thank you very much.
